newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Police stop Tirana rally, protests elsewhere.
newsitem.headline: Police stop Tirana rally, protests elsewhere.

text.p: Albanian police headed off an anti-government rally in the capital on Sunday but thousands of beggared investors marched elsewhere to demand compensation for heavy losses in failed pyramid investment schemes.
Investors in three southern towns held protests again on Sunday, ignoring government appeals to shrug off millions of dollars in losses and get back to work.
The protesters in Fier, Vlore and Sarande chanted slogans against the right-wing government of Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi and President Sali Berisha and demanded compensation for losses.
In Fier, 2,000 protesters denounced Berisha and carried local opposition Socialist Party leader Petro Koci through the streets on their shoulders.
"There is a war between Fier residents and Berisha. Be assured we will win," Koci told the crowd.
The protests were quieter than in recent days and no riot police were seen, part of a new strategy by the government to let marches go ahead unopposed outside the capital.
Police set up roadblocks between Fier, south of Tirana, and Vlore, on the coast further south, turning back demonstrators who tried to move between the two towns.
Albania, Europe's poorest state, has been swept by protests and riots over the past month after five hugely popular pyramid investment schemes collapsed owing millions of dollars.

Angry investors, many of whom earned their money as illegal workers in neighbouring European Union states, blame Meksi and Berisha for failing to warn them about the dangers of the unregulated schemes.
Most of the schemes promoted an image of being part of an Albanian economic boom, allegedly building resorts, supermarkets and petrol stations, but they were in fact pocketing cash.
Economists and diplomats estimate $1 to $2 billion were in the failed schemes. Four others have kept paying interest but have frozen clients' capital.
Many among Albania's 3.4 million people were invested in the schemes. In extreme cases people sold homes and valuables in a frenzy to invest before the schemes collapsed.

Albania, which for 45 years lived in isolation and under a ruthless Stalinist government, emerged from communism in 1990. The pyramid crisis is the most serious challenge to the pro-market Democrats since they were elected in 1992.
In Tirana, police put on a show of force to ensure a rally called by the main opposition Forum for Democracy on Sunday did not take place.
A dozen police vans and cars cruised the area and officers moved quickly to make sure people kept going and did not loiter near the football stadium where the rally was due to be held.
Officers forced customers in nearby cafes out into a heavy rain storm to make sure that if any were potential protesters they would disperse or get drenched.
Berisha admitted on Saturday that it had been a mistake to use riot police against protesters and told reporters protests would be allowed in Tirana, too, if organisers had a permit.
But Sunday's actions showed the government is still loathe to let demonstrations take place in the capital and was hoping protests in the countryside would diminish.
Berisha acknowledged on Saturday that the government had committed errors and had warned the public too late about the dangers of the schemes.
But he said responsibility also lay with those who had put millions of dollars into the high-interest schemes -- and lost everything.
He stressed that the state had no intention of reimbursing hundreds of thousands of Albanians who lost their savings.
"We will not take this debt on our shoulders. No democratic government would do this. It would be cheating, printing money to pay and creating hyperinflation", he said.
Berisha acknowledged that many Albanians were now homeless, having sold houses or flats to invest in the schemes which paid interest of 60 percent or more a month.
But he said there was no question of elections because of the scandal. Meksi has made clear that he has no plans to quit and has taken a tough line throughout the crisis.
"At the moment the only way for Albanians to get back their money back ... is to work," he said at the weekend.
